thesis: Three different Pfizer insiders bought their own stock on the open market inside three weeks in August — the CEO for $1.0M at $26.34, and two directors for roughly $1.9M between them at $25.52 and $25.46 — and one of those directors ran Vanguard, which is not a person who buys a single stock casually. Executives sell for a hundred reasons and buy for one, and a cluster of distinct buyers at similar size in a narrow window is one of the few public signals with real predictive content. It lands on a business the market has priced for permanent post-patent-cliff decline, which is exactly the setup where insider conviction is worth the most: it is evidence that the people who can see the pipeline think the de-rating overshot.
key_risk: The insider cluster is the thesis, and insider buying is a probabilistic signal with a long lag — Bourla and the board can be right about the business and still be early by two years, and none of the three has been proven right yet at 27.94. The underlying problem is unchanged and large: Pfizer faces a patent cliff, and if the pipeline does not replace the revenue, no multiple is low enough. There is no hard stop on this position by design, so the $23 bear case — 17.7% below the market and just below the 23.62 ninety-day low — is a real drawdown that would not trigger any exit.
counter_argument: The strongest case against: the stock has already moved 8.3% off this report entry and is only 2.5% off its ninety-day high of 28.745, so the discount the insiders bought at has largely closed and the easy part of this trade has been taken. Insider buys of $1M by a CEO whose compensation runs far larger are cheap signalling, and a board that wanted to signal confidence into a de-rating would do exactly this whether or not the pipeline works. Buying at 27.94 is paying 8-10% more than three people with better information were willing to pay three weeks ago.

Revenue fell 5.5% year over year and first-half free cash flow was DOWN year over year, so the cash that services the debt is going the wrong way while the debt is being paid with asset sales rather than operations. thesis: This position now has both a dated mechanical bid and a resolved event risk. The Treasury said on 2026-08-19 it would at least double long-dated buybacks from $2B to $4B per operation between 2026-09-09 and 2026-11-04, which is an official bid of known size arriving on known dates. The event that could have overwhelmed it happened this morning and went the right way: Warsh told Jackson Hole that better summer inflation readings do not tell him underlying trends have meaningfully improved, and the curve bull-flattened — the 2-year jumped 6-8bp to 4.298-4.31%, its highest since late July, while the 30-year fell 2bp to 5.168%. That is the market paying the long end for Fed credibility. Going in, SocGen chief US economist Jan Groen warned that a speech without any hint that hikes remained on the table would read dovish and push the 30-year to 5.5% or above; Warsh delivered the opposite, so the specific tail risk this trade was carrying has been taken off the table rather than merely deferred.
key_risk: The long end has barely moved on all of this — TLT is 83.08, down 0.06% on the day, so the bull-flattening is 2 basis points and it is being read as more than it is. A hawkish Fed that actually hikes is not automatically good for a 20-year bond fund: if Warsh follows through, the whole curve can reprice upward and TLT falls with it. This same catalyst has already been faded once — yields rebounded on 08-20 and wiped out the entire post-buyback-announcement decline — and $4B per operation is small against the long-bond market if a fiscal repricing is what is really happening. The 80.95 stop is 2.6% away, which is about 3 ATR on a 0.84% ATR instrument, so it is a real stop rather than a noise stop, but it will close this before any of the buybacks conclude.
counter_argument: The strongest case against: the 30-year at 5.168% is still the highest since 2007, and it got there on persistent inflation and rising government debt, neither of which a hawkish speech or a $4B buyback fixes. The Treasury buying back its own long bonds with money it must first borrow is a rearrangement rather than a retirement, and the market voted on that within a day of the announcement. A Fed chair who refuses to give a reaction function is also a source of term premium in his own right — uncertainty about the path is exactly what investors demand compensation for at the long end.

That case is real, and it is the reason the position is being held at all rather than sold.

thesis: This is a continuing position, not a new idea, and the evidence under it is genuinely two-sided. The good part is hard numbers: Cameco raised 2026 revenue guidance to C$3.32-3.57B from C$2.85-3.06B on unchanged production of 19.5-21.5 million pounds, which is a pure price effect, and the average realised uranium price was $67.79/lb in Q2, up 18% from $57.35 a year earlier. The reconciling event is the confidential S-1 — an IPO would mark Westinghouse to a public price rather than leaving it as a line item that just went negative.
key_risk: The 29% run from 86.38 on 07-31 to 111.54 on 08-26 was driven by a trade-policy narrative — Cameco owns the refinery at the centre of a Canadian uranium export threat — and narrative-driven moves give back as fast as they arrive, which is what the -5.7% today looks like. Underneath it, 49% of the earnings story deteriorated sharply: Westinghouse went from +$126M to -$10M and took group adjusted EBITDA down 42%. There is no hard stop on a name with a 3.45% ATR, and the $86 bear case is a price the stock actually traded four weeks ago, so it is reachable in weeks. Insider data shows zero open-market purchases by anyone in six months, so there is no insider confirmation under this.
counter_argument: The strongest case against: the raised revenue guidance is a uranium price pass-through, not a volume or share gain, and the thing Cameco was supposed to be — a nuclear-renaissance compounder with a reactor business attached — just posted a loss in the reactor business. Buying at 100 means paying for a 29% run that a trade-policy headline created, on an asset whose 49% stake is being prepared for sale to public markets precisely when its earnings have inverted. If the Canadian export threat de-escalates, the narrative half of this price disappears and $86 is not a bear case but a return to where the fundamentals last supported it.
